paragraphs: This paper studies when proximal ADMM converges for optimization problems whose variables are divided into multiple blocks. Its focus is a particular arrangement of linear constraints, called block anti-upper triangular structure. Existing analyses often combine all constraints into one matrix and require properties of that entire matrix, such as full column rank.

That approach leaves a gap: some problems with this block structure can be solved by ADMM even though they fail the usual matrix assumptions. The authors introduce a new assumption that supports a convergence analysis attentive to the constraint structure. Under this assumption, they establish global convergence for the nonconvex setting.

For strongly convex problems, the paper also establishes global convergence and proves linear convergence in four different scenarios. Linear convergence describes a rate at which error contracts as iterations proceed. These results broaden the theoretical coverage of multiblock proximal ADMM; the guarantees remain tied to the stated assumptions and scenarios, rather than applying to every problem with multiple variable blocks.
icml-2026-a-proximal-admm-for-multiblock.tldr: A new convergence analysis extends proximal ADMM guarantees to structured multiblock problems that can fall outside standard matrix assumptions.

paragraphs: The paper addresses spatial reasoning in vision-language models by giving them a persistent representation of a scene. The authors argue that treating a model as a passive observer is restrictive, while reinforcement learning provides too little guidance when rewards arrive only sparsely. Their approach draws inspiration from how pigeons construct and use cognitive maps.

A dynamic cognitive map records object positions and orientations and serves as memory for incoming observations. The model also uses Spatial Assertion Codes: Python expressions that describe spatial relationships. Checking these expressions against the map makes intermediate reasoning steps verifiable, providing denser training rewards. The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement fine-tuning.

On MindCube, the approach achieves a reported state-of-the-art overall accuracy of 80.5%. On the difficult Rotation subset, it exceeds the best current method by 29.5 accuracy points, corresponding to a 53.2% relative improvement. These findings support the value of combining scene memory with checkable intermediate reasoning for the spatial tasks evaluated.
icml-2026-active-exploring-like-a-pigeon.tldr: A persistent spatial map and executable relationship checks provide denser training feedback, improving vision-language spatial reasoning on MindCube.

paragraphs: Code-generation systems trained with reinforcement learning can exploit their reward environments, making the reliability of evaluators important. This paper examines whether language models can detect such reward hacks. It introduces a taxonomy containing 54 exploit categories and TRACE, a benchmark of 517 synthetically constructed testing trajectories that were verified by humans.

The central comparison concerns how detection is presented. Instead of judging each trajectory alone, a contrastive setup lets evaluators analyze trajectories in relation to others. Models detect hacks more effectively in this setting. GPT-5.2 at its highest reasoning setting achieves the best reported detection rate, rising from 45% in isolated evaluation to 63% in contrastive evaluation on TRACE.

The study also finds that hacks requiring semantic context are substantially harder to identify than those contextualized syntactically. Detection changes with the proportion of benign and hacked trajectories and the size of analysis groups. These findings show that evaluation context materially affects measured detection ability, while the released benchmark and harness support further investigation.
icml-2026-benchmarking-reward-hack-detec.tldr: TRACE shows that comparing code trajectories improves reward-hack detection, although semantically contextualized exploits remain especially difficult.

paragraphs: CoFrGeNet explores whether language-generation models can retain strong performance with smaller alternatives to standard Transformer components. Inspired by continued fractions, the authors introduce a new family of functions and build components that can replace multi-head attention and feed-forward networks. These replacements require substantially fewer parameters.

The work also derives custom gradient formulas intended to optimize the new components more accurately and efficiently than standard PyTorch gradients. The components fit into existing Transformer training and inference procedures with little modification. This makes the proposal an architectural substitution that can use established workflows, alongside its mathematical contribution.

Experiments use GPT2-xl and Llama3 architectures, with pretraining on the datasets described in the abstract. Across classification, question answering, reasoning, and text understanding, the resulting models are competitive and sometimes outperform the originals while using roughly half to two-thirds as many parameters and less pretraining time. Additional benefits from hardware-specific implementations are presented as a future possibility, rather than an established experimental result.
icml-2026-cofrgenet-continued-fraction-a.tldr: Continued-fraction-inspired Transformer replacements deliver competitive language-task performance with fewer parameters and shorter pretraining in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Survival modeling can be difficult when events are rare or information is only partially observed. Biomedical studies may also involve expensive covariates, structured sampling, or parameters removed through conditioning. External predictive models could help, but existing distillation approaches often expect a fully specified likelihood or an explicit probability model for the outcome.

The paper develops knowledge distillation around composite likelihoods, which combine separate likelihood components without necessarily defining one global outcome distribution. Its key observation is that each component still defines a valid probability model over a restricted outcome space. This makes it possible to measure teacher-student disagreement using a principled Kullback–Leibler divergence within individual components.

The resulting framework transfers external predictive information without requiring access to external individual-level records. Simulations and biomedical case studies report better discrimination and predictive accuracy in settings with rare events and heterogeneous information. The contribution is therefore a way to perform distillation when the model specifies useful pieces of the outcome process without specifying its complete distribution.
icml-2026-component-wise-composite-likel.tldr: Component-level probability models enable principled knowledge distillation for survival settings without fully specified outcome distributions.

paragraphs: ConPress starts from an observed behavior of large reasoning models: when several independent, answerable questions appear in one prompt, the model tends to produce shorter reasoning for each. The authors call this self-compression and report that it recurs across models and benchmarks. They attribute it to pressure created by sharing the prompt context across questions.

The training method turns that behavior into examples. It constructs multi-question prompts, samples the model's responses, then separates and filters the reasoning for individual questions to retain concise, correct trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning on those trajectories teaches the model to use compressed reasoning even when it later receives a single question.

This process requires no external teacher, manual trace pruning, or reinforcement learning. With 8,000 fine-tuning examples, the reported reasoning-token reductions are 59% on MATH500 and 33% on AIME25, with competitive accuracy. The findings suggest that a model's own context-induced behavior can supply useful training data for reducing reasoning overhead; competitive accuracy does not imply that accuracy is identical in every setting.
icml-2026-conpress-learning-efficient-re.tldr: ConPress trains on concise reasoning elicited by multi-question prompts, reducing reasoning-token use while maintaining competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: AI-generated annotations are fast and inexpensive, but asking a model to judge them can leave its judgments without reliable reference points. SAGE addresses this by retrieving semantically similar samples with nearest-neighbor search and using them as references when checking an annotation. The paper studies both the method and the conditions under which these references help.

Its theoretical framework expresses error-detection AUROC through three factors: how distinguishable correct and incorrect annotations already are, how references shift their scores, and how averaging reduces noise. This decomposition explains the proposed calibration effect: suitable references can raise scores for correct annotations while lowering scores for incorrect ones.

The benefit is conditional on references being semantically matched and correct. Experiments involving language generation, image captioning, and classification support improved detection when neighbors provide reliable calibration. The analysis also helps identify circumstances where direct scoring or another strategy may be preferable. The contribution is therefore both a reference-based detector and an explanation of why retrieving similar examples is not automatically beneficial.
icml-2026-detecting-errors-in-ai-generat.tldr: SAGE improves annotation-error detection when retrieved neighbors are both semantically relevant and correct, with theory explaining that conditional benefit.

paragraphs: Predicting time to an event becomes harder when events are rare and several event types compete. Censoring adds another complication because some observations provide only partial outcome information. DiSKD addresses how an external predictive model can help a local model in this setting, including when their definitions of outcomes do not align exactly.

The framework works in discrete time and transfers teacher predictions through a Kullback–Leibler divergence that varies by event cause and time. This gives the transfer mechanism a structure suited to competing risks. It also adapts the strength of teacher guidance, placing more weight on compatible teachers and less on teachers whose information is less relevant.

The authors report robustness to model misspecification and differences in outcome definitions, alongside improved discrimination and calibration in simulations and real-world applications. Those improvements concern both distinguishing outcomes and making probabilities agree with observed outcomes. Because transfer uses predictions without requiring raw-data sharing, the framework offers a privacy-conscious route to incorporating external information, without the abstract claiming a formal privacy guarantee.
icml-2026-discrete-survival-knowledge-di.tldr: DiSKD transfers external predictions into competing-risk survival models using cause- and time-specific guidance that adapts to teacher compatibility.

paragraphs: Graph mixture-of-experts models aim to assign different graph patterns to different specialist networks. The paper identifies two obstacles to that goal. Experts can become too similar while the router concentrates assignments on only a few of them. Routers also frequently make uncertain assignments, and the authors observe a strong negative correlation between that uncertainty and model performance.

C²GMoE addresses routing with a group-wise contrastive strategy. It guides node assignments using semantic clusters while also enforcing load-balancing constraints. The purpose is to give routing a meaningful basis for distinguishing nodes and specialists, while avoiding concentration of work in a small subset of experts.

The framework separately changes how expert predictions are combined. A confidence-aware fusion mechanism, motivated by an analysis of generalization error, adjusts each expert's contribution according to its confidence. Experiments across multiple benchmarks support the overall method's effectiveness. Together, the components address both which experts receive a node and how their predictions contribute to its final result.
icml-2026-discriminative-mixture-of-expe.tldr: C²GMoE combines semantically guided routing with confidence-weighted predictions to improve coordination among graph experts.

paragraphs: HySCAN targets two aspects of adversarial robustness: mathematically certified protection under an l2 measure and observed resistance to strong attacks under an l-infinity measure. These evaluate different properties of a defense. The paper aims to narrow the gap between them while preserving performance on ordinary, unperturbed images.

The approach combines randomness in two parts of the model. Stochastic-aware random weights introduce randomness at the parameter level, while stochastic attention noise modules introduce it into internal feature representations. The framework uses these complementary sources during training and inference, seeking both meaningful certificates and stronger practical resistance to attacks.

Experiments span several imaging datasets, including CelebA, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, HAM10000, and NIH Chest X-ray. The authors report improvements over existing certified and empirical defenses of up to approximately 9.6% in certified robustness and 5% in empirical robustness, without reducing clean accuracy. These are maximum reported improvements across the experiments, supporting the combined design without establishing equal gains for every dataset or attack.
icml-2026-does-a-hybrid-space-aware-rand.tldr: HySCAN combines parameter and feature randomness to improve certified and empirical adversarial robustness without reducing clean accuracy in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Predicting protein fitness from sequence is useful only if models remain effective under the data changes encountered in protein engineering. The paper argues that this generalization remains uncertain in practice. The earlier FLIP benchmark tested some distribution shifts, but its measurements covered stability, binding, and viral capsid viability.

FLIP2 expands that evaluation with seven new datasets, including enzymes, protein-protein interactions, and light-sensitive proteins. It also introduces data splits intended to test generalization relevant to real engineering campaigns. These splits make the benchmark about performance under meaningful shifts in available data, alongside the broader range of protein settings.

Across the evaluated datasets and test suites, simpler models often match or outperform fine-tuned protein language models. This result questions how reliably existing transfer-learning methods deliver practical advantages in these settings; it does not establish that simpler models always win. The authors record dataset provenance and redistribute the data under CC-BY 4.0, supporting continued comparisons using a shared, documented resource.
icml-2026-flip2-expanding-protein-fitnes.tldr: FLIP2 broadens realistic protein-fitness evaluation and finds that simpler models often rival or outperform fine-tuned protein language models.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models store large collections of expert parameters, creating a substantial memory burden. Mixed-precision quantization reduces that burden by giving different experts different numerical bit widths. The challenge is deciding where precision matters most while accounting for the fact that quantization can change which experts the router should select.

GEMQ treats bit allocation as a model-wide problem. It uses quantization-error analysis to estimate expert importance and formulates allocation through linear programming. It also fine-tunes the router so that routing adapts to the quantized experts. This addresses both numerical changes within experts and the decisions that determine how those experts are used.

The two components operate progressively, with importance estimates and precision assignments refined over successive quantization stages. Experiments report substantial memory reduction and faster inference with minimal accuracy degradation. The findings support coordinating compression and routing across the whole model, because choosing precision using only layer-level importance can overlook interactions that matter after experts have been quantized.
icml-2026-gemq-global-expert-level-mixed.tldr: GEMQ jointly refines model-wide expert precision and routing to reduce MoE memory and inference costs with minimal reported accuracy loss.

paragraphs: LASER studies how to reconstruct a physical field when measurements are sparse and sensing is constrained. Fixed sensor layouts cannot respond as the underlying physical state evolves. The proposed framework instead links reconstruction and sensor movement in a closed loop, allowing sensing decisions to depend on the system's changing estimated state.

The authors formulate this process as a partially observable decision problem. A latent world model represents the physical field's dynamics and supplies an internal reward signal. A reinforcement learning policy uses this model to explore hypothetical sensing actions in its compressed representation, considering what different movements might reveal before selecting an action.

Sensor movements are conditioned on predicted latent states, helping the policy seek potentially informative regions beyond what has already been observed. Across diverse continuum fields, experiments report consistently better reconstruction than static and offline-optimized sensing strategies under sparse measurements. The results support the value of adapting measurements during reconstruction, with the learned dynamics model connecting current observations to possible future sensing choices.
icml-2026-laser-learning-active-sensing-.tldr: LASER uses a learned dynamics model to plan sensor movements, improving sparse physical-field reconstruction over static and offline-optimized strategies.

paragraphs: This paper addresses vision-language hallucinations by making visual differences an explicit part of training. It identifies two problems with existing visual preference approaches: their objectives can compare quantities with mismatched normalization, and their negative images can differ so broadly that models learn shortcuts instead of attending to precise semantic differences.

IC-VCO places contrasting images together within one shared context, providing a mathematically consistent comparison objective. An additional regularizer, Visual Contrast Distillation, encourages agreement between multi-image contrastive training and the single-image setting used at inference. A reliability gate controls this auxiliary guidance, connecting the training setup to the conditions in which the model will later operate.

The paper also edits contrastive samples through precise semantic perturbations to produce difficult negatives. These examples make fine visual discrepancies central to learning. Across five benchmarks, the authors report the best overall performance for IC-VCO and evidence that the editing strategy is effective. The contribution combines objective design, training-to-inference consistency, and more targeted visual supervision.
icml-2026-learning-from-fine-grained-vis.tldr: IC-VCO uses shared-context image comparisons and precise visual edits to improve training against multimodal hallucinations.

paragraphs: Long-context Transformers face a cost problem because softmax attention scales quadratically with sequence length. Linear attention reduces that expense by compressing past keys and values into a fixed-size hidden state, but the state's limited capacity restricts expressivity. Earlier hybrid designs mix entire softmax and linear-attention layers, leaving softmax layers as a computational bottleneck.

NAtS-L moves the choice inside each layer, assigning different tokens to different attention operations. The framework determines which tokens can be handled through compressed linear-attention state and which should remain available for later softmax retrieval. The intended distinction is between information with short-term influence and information needed by future queries.

The authors search for token-level combinations of Gated DeltaNet and softmax attention and report a strong, efficient hybrid architecture. Its significance is the finer granularity of resource allocation: a layer does not need to apply the same attention mechanism to every token. The stated results support adapting the mechanism to tokens' information roles within the sequence.
icml-2026-neural-attention-search-linear.tldr: NAtS-L assigns linear or softmax attention to individual tokens within a layer to balance compression, retrieval, and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Operator splitting tackles a difficult optimization problem through simpler subproblems, often expressed as proximal operations. Its practical reach is restricted when those operations lack closed-form solutions. This paper studies how numerical approximations can fill that gap while retaining convergence guarantees for the surrounding optimization algorithm.

The approximation is HJ-Prox, a derivative-free Monte Carlo method derived from Hamilton–Jacobi partial differential equation theory. The authors place it inside a unified operator-splitting framework. This permits approximate proximal steps for functions that are not directly proximable, extending the range of problems to which these methods can be applied.

Under assumptions described as mild, the paper proves convergence is preserved for several algorithms, including proximal point, proximal gradient descent, Douglas–Rachford, Davis–Yin, and primal–dual hybrid gradient. Numerical experiments report competitive and effective performance across statistical learning tasks. The central result is that using sampled numerical proximal approximations can be theoretically justified across multiple splitting schemes, provided the relevant assumptions hold.
icml-2026-operator-splitting-with-hamilt.tldr: A unified framework uses HJ-Prox numerical approximations to extend operator splitting while preserving convergence under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: Many learned simulators produce a single deterministic forecast, even when the physical dynamics are chaotic or uncertain. Training a probabilistic replacement from the beginning can be expensive. This paper instead adapts existing deterministic models so that prior investment in their predictive capabilities can support probabilistic simulation.

The retrofitting procedure trains with the Continuous Ranked Probability Score, a proper scoring rule for probabilistic predictions. The same adaptation mechanism works across different backbone architectures with minimal code changes. The authors test both models pretrained on individual dynamical systems and a PDE foundation model pretrained across multiple systems.

For single-system models, rollout CRPS falls by 20–54% and variance-normalized RMSE improves by up to 30% relative to compute-matched deterministic fine-tuning. For the foundation model, the reported improvements reach 40% in CRPS and 15% in variance-normalized RMSE compared with deterministic fine-tuning. These results show that the tested backbones can gain useful probabilistic behavior with modest additional training, while also improving the reported point-prediction error measure.
icml-2026-probabilistic-retrofitting-of-.tldr: Retrofitting pretrained deterministic simulators with a probabilistic scoring rule improves uncertainty-sensitive and prediction-error metrics with modest additional training.

paragraphs: The paper examines whether generated robot videos depict correct tasks and physically realistic behavior. It introduces RBench, an evaluation resource spanning five task domains and four robot embodiments. Reproducible metrics assess task correctness alongside visual fidelity, making the benchmark useful for examining more than how convincing a video looks.

An evaluation of 25 models reveals substantial shortcomings in physical realism. RBench's reported Spearman correlation of 0.96 with human judgment indicates strong agreement in ranking within that evaluation. The benchmark therefore supplies evidence of deficiencies and a standardized way to measure progress toward addressing them.

The authors also tackle training-data scarcity with a four-stage pipeline that produces RoVid-X, containing four million annotated robotic video clips across thousands of tasks, including physical-property annotations. They describe it as the largest open-source robotic dataset for video generation. Fine-tuning on RoVid-X produces consistent gains in the reported experiments. Together, the benchmark and dataset connect measurement of robot-video quality with a resource for improving it.
icml-2026-rethinking-video-generation-mo.tldr: RBench exposes physical-realism gaps in robot video generation, while the four-million-clip RoVid-X dataset supports consistent fine-tuning gains.

paragraphs: RMNP addresses the computational cost of preconditioning during neural-network training. Preconditioning reshapes optimization updates to account for the loss landscape. Muon performs this through Newton–Schulz iterations without constructing the preconditioning matrix explicitly. The proposed optimizer replaces those iterations with a simpler normalization of momentum rows along the input dimension.

The substitution is motivated by an empirically observed diagonal-block structure in Transformer layer Hessians. The authors also report empirical verification of asymptotic equivalence between orthogonalization and the chosen row normalization in Transformers. For an m-by-n weight matrix, the stated per-iteration cost drops from O(mn min(m,n)) to O(mn).

The paper provides nonconvex convergence guarantees matching recent Muon results and achieving the stated minimax-optimal complexity. Large-language-model pretraining experiments show competitive optimization performance with substantially less wall-clock time spent on preconditioning. The theoretical guarantees and empirical Transformer observations play distinct roles: the former support convergence, while the latter motivate why this inexpensive substitution can retain useful optimization behavior in the tested setting.
icml-2026-rmnp-row-momentum-normalized-p.tldr: RMNP replaces Muon's iterative preconditioning with row normalization, reducing computational cost while retaining competitive reported optimization performance.

paragraphs: This paper studies estimating a distribution's mean when an adversary replaces a small constant fraction of observations with samples from shifted copies of the same distribution. The shifts can be arbitrary, but the replacement distributions retain this structural relationship to the original. Earlier work established sample-complexity results for Gaussian and Laplace base distributions.

The authors extend the analysis to more general base distributions, including multivariate ones. Under mild spectral conditions on the distribution's characteristic function, they show that a sample-efficient algorithm can estimate the target mean to any desired accuracy. The conditions are central to the result: the guarantee is for distributions satisfying them.

A qualitatively matching lower bound complements the algorithmic upper bound, helping characterize how many samples the task requires. Both arguments rely on Fourier analysis and a newly introduced Fourier witness. The results substantially resolve the stated open question and clarify how structured mean-shift contamination can permit consistent estimation, unlike the impossibility established for the broader Huber contamination model.
icml-2026-sample-complexity-bounds-for-r.tldr: Under spectral conditions, Fourier-based analysis establishes sample-efficient mean estimation under mean-shift contamination and a qualitatively matching lower bound.

paragraphs: SciVideoBench evaluates whether multimodal models can reason about scientific experimental videos. The paper argues that general video benchmarks rely heavily on recognition and relatively simple reasoning, allowing performance to saturate without adequately testing more demanding abilities. Scientific experiments provide a setting where understanding what appears on screen must connect to specialized knowledge.

The benchmark contains 1,000 multiple-choice questions drawn from experimental videos across more than 25 academic subjects and checked with a semi-automatic verification system. Its questions require domain knowledge, precise perception of spatial and temporal relationships, and complex logical reasoning. This combination makes the task depend on both scientific understanding and evidence in the video.

Evaluations of proprietary and open-source models, including Gemini 2.5 Pro and Qwen2.5-VL, reveal substantial performance deficits. Analyses examine factors such as reasoning complexity and visual grounding to help explain the difficulty. The benchmark supplies a more demanding test of scientific video reasoning and identifies capabilities that still need improvement in the evaluated models.
icml-2026-scivideobench-benchmarking-sci.tldr: SciVideoBench uses scientific experiment videos to expose gaps in multimodal models' domain knowledge, visual grounding, and complex reasoning.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why text encoders have not scaled like decoders. Using probes with frozen backbones, the authors find that BERT representations become harder for those probes to exploit even as perplexity improves. This exposes a mismatch between improving token reconstruction and producing representations useful under the frozen evaluation setup.

CrossBERT addresses the mismatch with a two-part architecture that separates representation learning from token reconstruction. The design allows masking ratios of at least 50%, while a Complementary Masking Strategy gathers gradients across all tokens. These mechanisms target training throughput and sample efficiency alongside the quality of the encoded representations.

The abstract reports throughput gains of 1.5–2 times and a twofold improvement in sample efficiency from these respective mechanisms. CrossBERT also shows monotonic scaling and superior results on MTEB English version 2 and frozen GLUE evaluations. The findings support separating the two learning roles when scaling encoders, with the original diagnosis specifically grounded in how usable representations are to frozen-backbone probes.
icml-2026-separating-representation-from.tldr: CrossBERT separates representation learning from token reconstruction, improving encoder scaling, throughput, and sample efficiency in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Communication helps cooperating agents compensate for incomplete observations and randomness, but possible pairwise connections grow rapidly as more agents join. SOPS separates two design questions: how to keep the communication structure scalable, and how to select links that help the current task. This avoids asking one unconstrained link-selection mechanism to solve both problems.

The framework first restricts candidate connections to an exponential-graph backbone. Each agent has only logarithmically many candidates, while the graph's small diameter preserves the possibility of rapid information mixing. A learned pairwise scoring network then uses agent states and edge-type embeddings to select a sparse, task-conditioned communication subgraph.

The selection mechanism uses a differentiable Gumbel–Sigmoid formulation so communication choices can be optimized end to end for return. Across cooperative benchmarks of different sizes, SOPS significantly outperforms the existing state-of-the-art methods considered and shows robust zero-shot transfer. These findings support combining a structurally efficient candidate network with learned allocation of the links actually used.
icml-2026-sparse-topology-aware-pairwise.tldr: SOPS combines a scalable communication backbone with learned sparse links to improve cooperation across multi-agent benchmarks.

paragraphs: Generating more candidate answers can help when an external verifier reliably rejects mistakes. This paper asks whether polling model answers can provide similar truthfulness gains when such verification is unavailable. Across five benchmarks and models, polling-style aggregation delivers no consistent accuracy improvement over a single sample, even at 25 times the inference cost.

The authors link this failure to correlated errors. Under uncertainty, models are better at anticipating other models' responses than at identifying the truth. Agreement therefore need not provide independent evidence of correctness. The study also finds correlated outputs across models when they receive out-of-distribution random strings and are asked for pseudo-random responses.

Weighting answers by self-reported confidence does not help in the reported experiments because confidence does not reliably separate correct and incorrect answers. The findings identify a limitation of the tested inference-scaling strategies: more samples supply useful candidates when verification works, but polling without a reliable truth signal can reinforce shared mistakes. They do not establish that every possible future aggregation method must fail.
icml-2026-truthfulness-does-not-scale-li.tldr: Across the tested models and benchmarks, polling more answers fails to consistently improve truthfulness because model errors and confidence are unreliable signals.

paragraphs: An agent can take an incorrect tool action when a user's instructions leave the intended goal unclear. This paper trains a language-model clarifier to ask questions that resolve that ambiguity. The central objective is to make clarification useful for completing the user's task, with question quality tied to the uncertainty the exchange removes.

The proposed Information Gain Reward measures how the clarification exchange updates a Bayesian belief toward the ground-truth goal. Training with this reward encourages the clarifier to elicit information that distinguishes the intended goal from alternatives. The reward connects a question's value to its effect on the agent's understanding within an environment involving tools and a user.

The framework is evaluated in a clarification-enhanced version of τ-Bench, with cross-agent testing across five heterogeneous backbones. The authors report a consistent 3.7% success-rate improvement over a no-clarification baseline, while adding only 0.3 total interaction steps on average. This suggests that targeted questions can improve task completion with a small average interaction cost in the evaluated setting.
icml-2026-uncertainty-aware-clarificatio.tldr: Training clarification questions for information gain improves agent task success with a small average increase in interaction steps.
